'''''Inception''''' is a 2010 <!--- Per [[WP: FILMLEAD]], do not add American-British or British-American: "If the nationality is not singular, cover the different national interests later in the lead section."---> [[science fiction action]] film written and directed by [[Christopher Nolan]], who also produced it with [[Emma Thomas]], his wife. The film stars [[Leonardo DiCaprio]] as a professional thief who steals information by infiltrating the [[subconscious]] of his targets. He is offered a chance to have his criminal history erased as payment for the implantation of another person's idea into a target's subconscious. The [[ensemble cast]] includes [[Ken Watanabe]], [[Joseph Gordon-Levitt]], [[Marion Cotillard]], [[Elliot Page]],{{efn|name=Elliot}} [[Tom Hardy]], [[Cillian Murphy]], [[Tom Berenger]], [[Dileep Rao]], and [[Michael Caine]].

After the completion of ''[[Insomnia (2002 film)|Insomnia]]'' in 2002, Nolan presented to [[Warner Bros. Pictures|Warner Bros.]] a written 80-page [[film treatment|treatment]] for a [[horror film]] envisioning "dream stealers," based on [[lucid dreaming]]. Deciding he needed more experience before tackling a production of this magnitude and complexity, Nolan shelved the project and instead worked on ''[[Batman Begins]]'' (2005), ''[[The Prestige]]'' (2006), and ''[[The Dark Knight]]'' (2008). The treatment was revised over six months and was purchased by Warner Bros. in February 2009. ''Inception'' was filmed in six countries, beginning in Tokyo on June 19 and ending in Canada on November 22. Its official budget was $160 million, split between Warner Bros. and [[Legendary Pictures|Legendary]]. Nolan's reputation and success with ''The Dark Knight'' helped secure the film's US$100 million in advertising expenditure.

''Inception''{{'}}s premiere was held in [[London]] on July 8, 2010; it was released in both conventional and [[IMAX]] theaters beginning on July 16, 2010. ''Inception'' grossed $839 million worldwide, becoming the [[2010 in film#Highest-grossing films|fourth-highest-grossing film of 2010]]. Considered one of the best films of the 2010s,<ref name="Metacritic 2010s">{{cite web|date=November 18, 2019|first=Jason|last=Dietz|url=https://www.metacritic.com/feature/best-movies-of-the-decade-2010s|title=The Best Movies of the Decade (2010–19), According to Film Critics|website=[[Metacritic]]|access-date=January 26, 2020|archive-date=January 1, 2020|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200101162640/https://www.metacritic.com/feature/best-movies-of-the-decade-2010s|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="Times">{{cite web | url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2025/movies/best-movies-21st-century.html | title=The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century | work=The New York Times | date=June 23, 2025 }}</ref> ''Inception'', among its [[List of accolades received by Inception|numerous accolades]], won four [[Academy Awards|Oscars]] ([[Academy Award for Best Cinematography|Best Cinematography]], [[Academy Award for Best Sound Editing|Best Sound Editing]], [[Academy Award for Best Sound|Best Sound Mixing]], [[Academy Award for Best Visual Effects|Best Visual Effects]]) and was nominated for four more ([[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]], [[Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay|Best Original Screenplay]], [[Academy Award for Best Production Design|Best Art Direction]], [[Academy Award for Best Original Score|Best Original Score]]) at the [[83rd Academy Awards]]. The [[Library of Congress]] selected ''Inception'' for preservation in the United States [[National Film Registry]]'s class of 2025 for being "culturally, historically or aesthetically significant".

== Plot ==
<!-- STOP!!! Do not add any unnecessary details to the plot. Per WP: FILMPLOT, the plot summary should be 400-700 words. Word count as of Sep 30, 2023 is 636. -->

Dom Cobb and Arthur are "extractors" who perform [[Industrial espionage|corporate espionage]] using experimental dream-sharing technology to infiltrate their targets' [[Unconscious mind|subconscious]] and extract information. Their latest target, Saito, is impressed with Cobb's ability to [[false awakening|layer multiple dreams within each other]]. He offers to hire Cobb for the ostensibly impossible job of implanting an idea into a person's subconscious; performing "inception" on Robert Fischer, the son of Saito's competitor Maurice Fischer, with the idea to dissolve his father's company. In return, Saito promises to clear Cobb's criminal status, allowing him to return home to his children.

Cobb accepts the offer and assembles his team: a forger named Eames, a chemist named Yusuf, and a college student named Ariadne. Ariadne is tasked with designing the dream's architecture, something Cobb himself cannot do for fear of being sabotaged by his mind's projection of his late wife, Mal. Maurice Fischer dies, and the team sedates Robert Fischer into a three-layer shared dream on an airplane to America bought by Saito. Time on each layer runs slower than the layer above, with one member staying behind on each to perform a music-synchronized "[[Hypnic jerk|kick]]" (using the French song "[[Non, je ne regrette rien]]") to awaken dreamers on all three levels simultaneously.

The team abducts Robert in a city on the first level, but unknown to any team member, his subconscious projections, trained to anticipate such a scenario, attack them. After Saito is wounded, Cobb reveals that while dying in the dream would usually awaken dreamers, Yusuf's sedatives will instead send them into "[[Limbo#Cultural references|Limbo]]": a world of infinite subconscious. Eames impersonates Robert's godfather, Peter Browning, to introduce the idea of an alternate will to dissolve the company.

Cobb explains to Ariadne that he and Mal entered Limbo while experimenting with dream-sharing, experiencing fifty years in one night due to the [[time dilation]] with reality. After waking up, Mal still believed she was dreaming. Attempting to "wake up," she committed suicide and framed Cobb for her murder to force him to do the same. Cobb fled the U.S., leaving his children behind.

Yusuf drives the team around the first level as they are sedated into the second level, a hotel dreamed by Arthur. Cobb persuades Robert that Browning has kidnapped him to stop the dissolution and that Cobb is a defensive projection, leading Robert to another third level deeper as part of a ruse to enter Robert's subconscious.

In the third level, the team infiltrates an alpine fortress with a projection of Maurice inside, where the inception itself can be performed. However, Yusuf performs his kick too soon by driving off a bridge, forcing Arthur and Eames to improvise a new set of kicks synchronized with them hitting the water by rigging an elevator and the fortress, respectively, with explosives. Mal then appears and kills Robert before he can be subjected to the inception; he and Saito are subsequently lost in Limbo, forcing Cobb and Ariadne to rescue them in time for Robert's inception and Eames's kick. Cobb reveals that during their time in Limbo, Mal refused to return to reality; Cobb had to convince her it was only a dream, accidentally incepting in her the belief that the real world was still a dream. Cobb makes peace with his part in Mal's death. Ariadne kills Mal's projection and wakes Robert up with a kick.

Revived into the third level, Robert discovers the planted idea: his dying father telling him to create something for himself. While Cobb searches for Saito in Limbo, the others ride the synced kicks back to reality. Cobb finds an aged Saito and reminds him of their agreement. The dreamers all awaken on the plane, and Saito makes a phone call. Arriving in [[Los Angeles International Airport|Los Angeles]], Cobb passes the immigration checkpoint, and his father-in-law accompanies him to his home. Cobb uses Mal's "totem" – a [[Spinning top|top]] that spins indefinitely in a dream – to test if he is indeed in the real world, but he chooses not to observe the result and instead joins his children.

== Cast ==
[[File: InceptionCastPremiereJuly10.jpg|thumb|upright=1.6|The cast at a premiere for the film in July 2010. From left to right: Cillian Murphy, Marion Cotillard, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Elliot Page, Ken Watanabe, Michael Caine, and Leonardo DiCaprio|alt=A man in a black suit, a woman in a pink dress, a man in a plaid suit, a woman in a black dress, a Japanese man in a black suit, and an old man in a blue suit clap their hands, while a man in a black suit stands. A microphone stand is in the foreground, and blue curtains are in the background.]]
* [[Leonardo DiCaprio]] as Dom Cobb, a professional thief who specializes in [[con artist|conning]] secrets from his victims by infiltrating their dreams. DiCaprio was the first actor to be cast in the film.<ref name="Weintraub" /> [[Brad Pitt]] and [[Will Smith]] were the first two choices and were offered the role, according to ''[[The Hollywood Reporter]]''.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/list-directors-43873 | work=The Hollywood Reporter | first=Kim | last=Masters | title=The A-List Directors | date=November 10, 2010 | access-date=April 17, 2020 | archive-date=July 17, 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200717145859/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/list-directors-43873 | url-status=live }}</ref> Smith turned it down because he didn't understand it.<ref>{{cite news |last=Sharf |first=Zack |url=https://variety.com/2025/film/news/will-smith-inception-offer-plot-confusing-1236432602/ |title=Will Smith Turned Down Christopher Nolan's 'Inception' Offer Because 'I Didn't Get It': 'Movies That Go Into Alternate Realities Don't Pitch Well' |work=Variety |date=June 15, 2025 |access-date=June 15, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250616013509/https://variety.com/2025/film/news/will-smith-inception-offer-plot-confusing-1236432602/ |archive-date=June 16, 2025 |url-status=live}}</ref> Cobb's role is compared to "the haunted widower in a Gothic romance".<ref>{{cite book |first=Charles |last=Burnetts |chapter='Downwards is the only way forwards': 'Dream Space,' Parallel Time and Selfhood in Inception |editor-last1=Jones|editor-first1=Matthew |editor-last2=Omrod |editor-first2=Joan |title=Time Travel in Popular Media: Essays on Film, Television, Literature and Video Games |location=[[Jefferson, North Carolina]] |publisher=[[McFarland & Company|McFarland]] |year=2015 |pages=234–246 |isbn=978-1-476-62008-4}}</ref>
* [[Ken Watanabe]] as Saito, a Japanese businessman who employs Cobb for the team's mission. Nolan wrote the role with Watanabe in mind, as he wanted to work with him again after ''[[Batman Begins]]''.<ref name="ProdNotes6-18" />{{rp|10}} ''Inception'' is Watanabe's first work in a contemporary setting where his primary language is English. Watanabe tried to emphasize a different characteristic of Saito in every dream level: "First chapter in my castle, I pick up some hidden feelings of the cycle. It's magical, powerful and then the first dream. And back to the second chapter, in the old hotel, I pick up [being] sharp and more calm and smart and it's a little bit [of a] different process to make up the character of any movie".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Billington |first=Alex |date=July 20, 2010 |title=Interview: Japanese Actor Ken Watanabe – Saito in Inception |website=FirstShowing.net |url=http://www.firstshowing.net/2010/interview-inceptions-saito-japanese-actor-ken-watanabe/ |url-status=live |access-date=July 3, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110827122953/http://www.firstshowing.net/2010/interview-inceptions-saito-japanese-actor-ken-watanabe/ |archive-date=August 27, 2011}}</ref>
* [[Joseph Gordon-Levitt]] as Arthur, Cobb's partner who manages and researches the missions. Gordon-Levitt compared Arthur to the producer of Cobb's art, "the one saying, 'Okay, you have your vision; now I'm going to figure out how to make all the nuts and bolts work so you can do your thing'".<ref name= ProdNotes6-18>{{cite web |url= http://wwws.warnerbros.co.uk/inception/mainsite/pdf/INCEPTION_PK_Notes__Bios_6-18.pdf |title=Production Notes 2010| website=Warner Bros. UK |access-date=September 1, 2014 |archive-date= November 10, 2014|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20141110071314/http://wwws.warnerbros.co.uk/inception/mainsite/pdf/INCEPTION_PK_Notes__Bios_6-18.pdf|url-status= live}}</ref>{{rp|7}} The actor did all but one of his stunt scenes and said the preparation "was a challenge and it would have to be for it to look real".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://video.about.com/movies/Joseph-Gordon-Levitt-Inception.htm |title=Joseph Gordon-Levitt Inception Interview |date=July 15, 2010 |first=Rebecca |last=Murray | website=[[About.com]] |access-date=July 3, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20111002051742/http://video.about.com/movies/Joseph-Gordon-Levitt-Inception.htm |archive-date=October 2, 2011}}</ref> [[James Franco]] was in talks with Christopher Nolan to play Arthur, but was ultimately unavailable due to scheduling conflicts.<ref>{{cite web|last=Rappe|first=Elisabeth|title=Christopher Nolan Trades James Franco for Joseph Gordon-Levitt in 'Inception'|date=April 24, 2009|website=MTV News |url=http://www.mtv.com/news/2431985/christopher-nolan-trades-james-franco-for-joseph-gordon-levitt-in-inception/ |access-date= June 23, 2016|archive-date=August 6, 2016|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160806000533/http://www.mtv.com/news/2431985/christopher-nolan-trades-james-franco-for-joseph-gordon-levitt-in-inception/ |url-status=dead}}</ref>
* [[Marion Cotillard]] as Mal, Cobb's deceased wife. She is a manifestation of Cobb's guilt about the real cause of Mal's suicide. He is unable to control these projections of her, challenging his abilities as an extractor.<ref name="threecircle" /> Nolan described Mal as "the essence of the [[femme fatale]]," and DiCaprio praised Cotillard's performance, saying that "she can be strong and vulnerable and hopeful and heartbreaking all in the same moment, which was perfect for all the contradictions of her character".<ref name="ProdNotes6-18" /> [[Kate Winslet]] was offered the role but turned it down as she couldn't see herself in the role.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sultan |first=Mahin |date=July 21, 2024 |title=Kate Winslet Turned Down Playing Leonardo DiCaprio's Lover for the 3rd Time in One of His Highest Grossing Movies That Sadly Never Happened |url=https://fandomwire.com/kate-winslet-turned-down-playing-leonardo-dicaprios-lover-for-the-3rd-time-in-one-of-his-highest-grossing-movies-that-sadly-never-happened/ |archive-date= |website=FandomWire}}</ref>
* [[Elliot Page]]{{efn|name=Elliot}} as Ariadne, a [[graduate student]] of architecture who is recruited to construct the various dreamscapes, which are described as mazes. The name [[Ariadne]] alludes to a princess of [[Greek mythology|Greek myth]], daughter of King [[Minos]], who aided the hero [[Theseus]] by giving him a sword and a ball of string to help him navigate the labyrinth which was the prison of the [[Minotaur]]. Nolan said that Page was chosen for being a "perfect combination of freshness and savvy and maturity" not common in people that age.<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|8}} Page said their character acts as a proxy to the audience, as "she's just learning about these ideas and, in essence, assists the audience in learning about dream sharing".<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/film/7868889/Inception-Ellen-Page-interview.html|title=Inception: Ellen Page interview|work=The Daily Telegraph|location=UK|first=Christine|last=Lennon|access-date=July 3, 2011|date=July 12, 2010|archive-date=October 23, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111023210948/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/film/7868889/Inception-Ellen-Page-interview.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The role was written with [[Evan Rachel Wood]] in mind, but she turned it down.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Chacksfield |first=Marc |date=October 22, 2014 |title=20 Things You (Probably) Didn't Know About Inception |url=https://www.shortlist.com/news/20-things-you-probably-didnt-know-about-inception |website=Shortlist}}</ref> [[Emily Blunt]], [[Rachel McAdams]], [[Taylor Swift]], [[Emma Roberts]], [[Jessy Schram]], and [[Carey Mulligan]] were also considered before it went to Page.<ref name=":0" />
* [[Tom Hardy]] as Eames, a sharp-tongued associate of Cobb. He is referred to as a [[Fence (criminal)|fence]] but his specialty is forgery, more accurately identity theft. Eames uses his ability to [[Impersonator|impersonate others]] inside the dream world in order to manipulate Fischer. Hardy described his character as "an old, [[Graham Greene]]-type diplomat; sort of faded, shabby, grandeur—the old Shakespeare lovey mixed with somebody from [[United Kingdom Special Forces|Her Majesty's Special Forces]]", who wears "campy, old money" costumes.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ugo.com/movies/diving-into-your-own-mind |title=Inception's Tom Hardy Is The Forger, Darling |website= [[UGO]].com |first=Matt |last=Patches |date=July 12, 2010 |access-date=July 3, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100905040047/http://www.ugo.com/movies/diving-into-your-own-mind |archive-date=September 5, 2010}}</ref>
* [[Cillian Murphy]] as Robert Fischer, the heir to a business empire and the team's target.<ref name="ProdNotes6-18" />{{rp|10}} Murphy said Fischer was portrayed as "a petulant child who's in need of a lot of attention from his father, he has everything he could ever want materially, but he's deeply lacking emotionally". The actor also researched the sons of [[Rupert Murdoch]], "to add to that the idea of living in the shadow of someone so immensely powerful".<ref>{{Cite web |last=O'Doherty |first=Cahir |date=July 15, 2010 |title=Hollywood golden boy Cillian Murphy talks about 'Inception' |url=http://www.irishcentral.com/IrishVoice/Hollywood-golden-boy-Cillian-Murphy-talks-about-Inception.html?page=2 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111011075823/http://www.irishcentral.com/IrishVoice/Hollywood-golden-boy-Cillian-Murphy-talks-about-Inception.html?page=2 |archive-date=October 11, 2011 |access-date=July 3, 2011 |work=Irish Voice Reporter}}</ref>
* [[Tom Berenger]] as Peter Browning, Robert Fischer's [[Godparent|godfather]] and fellow executive at the Fischers' company.<ref name="CinemaRewind">{{Cite web |author=George |date=July 23, 2009 |title=Hans Zimmer and Tom Berenger Join Inception |url=http://www.cinemarewind.com/2009/07/inception-cast-and-crew-updates.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090801155642/http://www.cinemarewind.com/2009/07/inception-cast-and-crew-updates.html |archive-date=August 1, 2009 |access-date=August 31, 2009 |work=CinemaRewind.com}}</ref> Berenger said Browning acts as a "surrogate father" to Fischer, who calls the character "Uncle Peter", and emphasized that "Browning has been with [Robert] his whole life and has probably spent more quality time with him than his own father".<ref name="ProdNotes6-18" />{{rp|11}}
* [[Michael Caine]] as Stephen Miles, Cobb's mentor and father-in-law,<ref name="ProdNotes6-18" />{{rp|11}} and Ariadne's college professor who recommends her to the team.<ref name="InContention">{{Cite news |last=Tapley |first=Kristopher |date=April 24, 2009 |title=Caine confirmed in small role in ''Inception'', Gordon-Levitt also joins the cast |website=InContention.com |url=https://incontention.com/?p=5843 |access-date=April 24, 2009 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120713015500/https://incontention.com/?p=5843 |archive-date=July 13, 2012}}</ref>
* [[Dileep Rao]] as Yusuf. Rao describes Yusuf as "an avant-garde pharmacologist, who is a resource for people, like Cobb, who want to do this work unsupervised, unregistered and unapproved of by anyone". Co-producer Jordan Goldberg said the role of the chemist was "particularly tough because you don't want him to seem like some kind of drug dealer", and that Rao was cast for being "funny, interesting and obviously smart".<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|11}}
* [[Lukas Haas]] as Nash, an architect in Cobb's employment who betrays the team and is later replaced by Ariadne.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Boursaw |first=Jane |date=August 26, 2009 |title=Ellen Page on the set of ''Inception'' in Paris |website=EveryJoe.com |url=http://everyjoe.com/entertainment/ellen-page-on-the-set-of-inception-in-paris/ |url-status=dead |access-date=August 26, 2009 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120712/http://everyjoe.com/entertainment/ellen-page-on-the-set-of-inception-in-paris/ |archive-date=July 12, 2012}}</ref>
* [[Talulah Riley]] as a woman, credited as "Blonde", whom Eames disguises himself as in a dream. Riley liked the role, despite it being minimal: "I get to wear a nice dress, pick up men in bars, and shove them in elevators. It was good to do something adultish. Usually I play 15-year-old English schoolgirls."<ref>{{cite web |author=Martin, Michael |date=May 10, 2010 |title=Talulah Riley |url=http://www.interviewmagazine.com/film/talulah-riley/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110929021125/http://www.interviewmagazine.com/film/talulah-riley/ |archive-date=September 29, 2011 |access-date=July 3, 2011 |work=[[Interview Magazine]]}}</ref>
* [[Pete Postlethwaite]] as Maurice Fischer, Robert Fischer's father and the dying founder of a business empire.

== Production ==

=== Development ===
[[File: Emma Thomas & Christopher Nolan at WonderCon 2010 1.JPG|thumb|left|upright=1.15|Emma Thomas and Christopher Nolan answer questions about ''Inception''. The husband-and-wife team produced the film through their company [[Syncopy Inc.|Syncopy]]. Nolan also wrote and directed it.]]
Initially, [[Christopher Nolan]] wrote an 80-page [[film treatment|treatment]] about dream-stealers.<ref name="Hiscock" /> Nolan had originally envisioned ''Inception'' as a [[horror film]],<ref name="Hiscock">{{Cite news|last=Hiscock|first=John|title=''Inception'': Christopher Nolan interview|work=Daily Telegraph|location=UK|date=July 1, 2010 |url= https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/film/filmmakersonfilm/7866677/Inception-Christopher-Nolan-interview.html|access-date=July 7, 2010|archive-date=July 4, 2010|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100704152719/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/film/filmmakersonfilm/7866677/Inception-Christopher-Nolan-interview.html|url-status=live}}</ref> but eventually wrote it as a [[heist film]] even though he found that "traditionally [they] are very deliberately superficial in emotional terms."<ref name="Boucher">{{Cite news| last= Boucher |first=Geoff|title=''Inception'' breaks into dreams|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=April 4, 2010|url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment/news/la-ca-inception4-2010apr04, 0,6869939.story|access-date=April 6, 2010|archive-date=November 21, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201121162456/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2010-apr-04-la-ca-inception4-2010apr04-story.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Upon revisiting his script, he decided that basing it in that genre did not work because the story "relies so heavily on the idea of the interior state, the idea of dream and [[memory]]. I realized I needed to raise the emotional stakes."<ref name="Boucher" />

Nolan worked on the script for nine to ten years.<ref name="Weintraub" /> When he first started thinking about making the film, Nolan was influenced by "that era of movies where you had ''[[The Matrix]]'' (1999), you had ''[[Dark City (1998 film)|Dark City]]'' (1998), you had ''[[The Thirteenth Floor]]'' (1999) and, to a certain extent, you had ''[[Memento (film)|Memento]]'' (2000), too. They were based in the principles that the world around you might not be real."<ref name="Boucher" /><ref>{{Cite web|date=July 16, 2010| first= Sheila |last= Marikar|title=Inside 'Inception': Could Christopher Nolan's Dream World Exist in Real Life? Dream Experts Say 'Inception's' Conception of the Subconscious Isn't Far From Science| publisher=[[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Entertainment/inside-inception-christopher-nolans-dream-world-exist-real/story?id=11174201|access-date=September 4, 2010| archive-date=April 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190430214607/https://abcnews.go.com/Entertainment/inside-inception-christopher-nolans-dream-world-exist-real/story?id=11174201|url-status=live}}</ref>

Nolan first [[Pitch (filmmaking)|pitched]] the film to [[Warner Bros. Pictures|Warner Bros.]] in 2001, but decided that he needed more experience making large-scale films and embarked on ''[[Batman Begins]]'' (2005) and ''[[The Dark Knight]]'' (2008).<ref name="Itzkoff">{{Cite news|last=Itzkoff|first=Dave|title=A Man and His Dream: Christopher Nolan and 'Inception'|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=June 30, 2010|url=https://artsbeat.blogs.nytimes.com/2010/06/30/a-man-and-his-dream-christopher-nolan-and-inception/|access-date=October 22, 2020|quote=This is a film I first pitched to the studio probably nine years ago, and I wasn't really ready to finish it. I needed more experience in making a big movie.|archive-date=March 24, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120324170554/http://artsbeat.blogs.nytimes.com/2010/06/30/a-man-and-his-dream-christopher-nolan-and-inception/|url-status=live}}</ref> He soon realized that a film like ''Inception'' needed a large budget because "as soon as you're talking about dreams, the potential of the human mind is infinite. And so the scale of the film has to feel infinite. It has to feel like you could go anywhere by the end of the film. And it has to work on a massive scale."<ref name="Itzkoff" /> After making ''The Dark Knight'', Nolan decided to make ''Inception'' and spent six months completing the script.<ref name="Itzkoff" /> Nolan said that the key to completing the script was wondering what would happen if several people shared the same dream. "Once you remove the privacy, you've created an infinite number of alternative universes in which people can meaningfully interact, with validity, with weight, with dramatic consequences."<ref name="Itzkoff2">{{Cite news| last= Itzkoff| first= Dave| title=The Man Behind the Dreamscape|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=June 30, 2010|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/07/04/movies/04inception.html|access-date=July 1, 2010 |archive-date=January 14, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120114141507/http://www.nytimes.com/2010/07/04/movies/04inception.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

Nolan had been trying to work with [[Leonardo DiCaprio]] for years and met him several times, but was unable to recruit him for any of his films until ''Inception''.<ref name="threecircle">{{Cite news|first=Borys |last=Kit |title=Three circle Nolan's 'Inception' |work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |date=April 1, 2009 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090406021957/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/hr/content_display/film/news/e3i7288557915e143d0665fd7eb397d74e8 |archive-date= April 6, 2009 |url= https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/hr/content_display/film/news/e3i7288557915e143d0665fd7eb397d74e8 |access-date=April 2, 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> DiCaprio finally agreed because he was "intrigued by this concept—this dream-heist notion and how this character's going to unlock his dreamworld and ultimately affect his real life."<ref name= Jolin>{{Cite news| last= Jolin |first= Dan |title= Crime of the Century |work=[[Empire (magazine)|Empire]]|date=July 2010}}</ref>{{rp|93–94}} He read the script and found it to be "very well written, comprehensive but you really had to have Chris in person, to try to articulate some of the things that have been swirling around his head for the last eight years."<ref name="Itzkoff" /> DiCaprio and Nolan spent months talking about the screenplay. Nolan took a long time re-writing the script in order "to make sure that the emotional journey of his [DiCaprio's] character was the driving force of the movie."<ref name="Weintraub" /> On February 11, 2009, it was announced that Warner Bros. purchased ''Inception'', a [[spec script]] written by Nolan.<ref name="first">{{Cite news|first=Michael|last=Fleming|url=https://variety.com/2009/film/features/nolan-tackles-inception-for-wb-1117999988/|title=Nolan tackles ''Inception'' for WB|work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=February 11, 2009|access-date=February 25, 2009|archive-date=November 14, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111114042446/http://www.variety.com/article/VR1117999988|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Locations and sets {{anchor|Filming}} ===
[[Principal photography]] began in [[Tokyo]] on June 19, 2009, with the scene in which Saito first hires Cobb during a helicopter flight over the city.<ref name="Hiscock" /><ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|13}}
[[File:Inception hallway fight scene.webm|thumb|right|Excerpt of the scene, visualizing the rotation of full 360 degrees in a [[gravity]] effect while in a hotel scene dreamed by Arthur]]

The production moved to the United Kingdom and shot in a converted [[airship hangar]] in [[Cardington, Bedfordshire|Cardington]], Bedfordshire, north of London.<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|14}} There, the hotel bar set which tilted 30 degrees was built.<ref name= Heuring>{{Cite news|last=Heuring|first=David|title=Dream Thieves|work=[[American Cinematographer]]|publisher=American Society of Cinematographers|date=July 2010|url=http://www.theasc.com/ac_magazine/July2010/Inception/page1.php|access-date=September 22, 2010|archive-date=September 22, 2010| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100922060626/http://www.theasc.com/ac_magazine/July2010/Inception/page1.php|url-status=live}}</ref>{{rp|29}} A hotel corridor was also constructed by [[Guy Hendrix Dyas]], the production designer, [[Chris Corbould]], the special effects supervisor, and [[Wally Pfister]], the director of photography; it rotated a full 360 degrees to create the effect of alternate directions of [[gravity]] for scenes set during the second level of dreaming, where dream-sector physics become chaotic. The idea was inspired by a technique used in [[Stanley Kubrick]]'s ''[[2001: A Space Odyssey (film)|2001: A Space Odyssey]]'' (1968). Nolan said, "I was interested in taking those ideas, techniques, and philosophies and applying them to an action scenario".<ref name= Heuring />{{rp|32}} The filmmakers originally planned to make the hallway only {{Convert|40|ft}} long, but as the action sequence became more elaborate, the hallway's length was increased to {{cvt|100|ft}}. The corridor was suspended along eight large concentric rings that were spaced equidistantly outside its walls and powered by two massive electric motors.<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|14}}

[[Joseph Gordon-Levitt]], who plays Arthur, spent several weeks learning to fight in a corridor that spun like "a giant [[hamster wheel]]".<ref name="Boucher" /> Nolan said of the device, "It was like some incredible torture device; we thrashed Joseph for weeks, but in the end we looked at the footage, and it looks unlike anything any of us has seen before. The rhythm of it is unique, and when you watch it, even if you know how it was done, it confuses your perceptions. It's unsettling in a wonderful way".<ref name="Boucher" /> Gordon-Levitt remembered, "it was six-day weeks of just, like, coming home at night battered ... The light fixtures on the ceiling are coming around on the floor, and you have to choose the right time to cross through them, and if you don't, you're going to fall."<ref>{{Cite news|last=Gordinier|first=Jeff|date=August 2010|title=Joseph Gordon-Levitt Comes of Age| page= 4|work=[[Details (magazine)|Details]]|url=http://www.details.com/celebrities-entertainment/cover-stars/201008/inception-actor-joseph-gordon-levitt|url-status=dead|access-date= July 27, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100709173118/http://www.details.com/celebrities-entertainment/cover-stars/201008/inception-actor-joseph-gordon-levitt| archive-date=July 9, 2010}}</ref> On July 15, 2009, filming took place at [[University College London]] for the sequences occurring inside a Paris college of architecture in the story,<ref name="Hiscock" /> including the library, Flaxman Gallery and Gustave Tuck Theatre.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.british-film-locations.com/Inception-2010|title=Where was 'Inception' filmed? – British Film Locations|work=British Film Locations|access-date=April 29, 2015|archive-date=September 23, 2015|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150923194624/http://www.british-film-locations.com/Inception-2010|url-status=live}}</ref>

Filming moved to France, where they shot Cobb entering the college of architecture (the place used for the entrance was the [[Musée Galliera]]) and the pivotal scenes between Ariadne and Cobb, in a [[bistro]] (a fictional one set up at the corner of Rue César Franck and Rue Bouchut), and lastly on the [[Pont de Bir-Hakeim|Bir-Hakeim bridge]].<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|17}} For the explosion that takes place during the bistro scene, local authorities would not allow the use of real explosives. High-pressure [[nitrogen]] was used to create the effect of a series of explosions. Pfister used six high-speed cameras to capture the sequence from different angles and make sure that they got the shot. The visual effects department enhanced the sequence, adding more destruction and flying debris. For the "Paris folding" sequence and when Ariadne "creates" the bridges, [[green screen]] and [[Computer-generated imagery|CGI]] were used on location.<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|17}}

[[Tangier]], Morocco, doubled as [[Mombasa]], where Cobb hires Eames and Yusuf. A foot chase was shot in the streets and alleyways of the historic [[medina quarter]].<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|18}} To capture this sequence, Pfister employed a mix of [[hand-held camera]] and [[steadicam]] work.<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|19}} Tangier was also used as the setting for filming an important riot scene during the initial foray into Saito's mind.

Filming moved to the [[Los Angeles]] area, where some sets were built on a Warner Bros. [[sound stage]], including the interior rooms of Saito's Japanese castle (the exterior was done on a small set built in [[Malibu Beach]]). The dining room was inspired by the historic [[Nijō Castle]], built around 1603. These sets were inspired by a mix of [[Japanese architecture]] and Western influences.<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|19}}

The production staged a multi-vehicle [[car chase]] on the streets of [[downtown Los Angeles]], which involved a freight train crashing down the middle of a street.<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|20}} To do this, the filmmakers configured a train engine on the chassis of a tractor trailer. The replica was made from [[fiberglass]] molds taken from authentic train parts and matched in terms of color and design.<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|21}} Also, the car chase was supposed to be set in the midst of a downpour, but the L.A. weather stayed typically sunny. The filmmakers set up elaborate effects (e.g., rooftop [[water cannon]]s) to give the audience the impression that the weather was overcast and soggy. L.A. was also the site of the climactic scene where a [[Ford Econoline]] van runs off the [[Schuyler Heim Bridge]] in slow motion.<ref name="Ditzian">{{Cite news| last= Ditzian |first= Eric |title=''Inception'' Stars Reveal Secrets Behind Epic Van Scene| website= MTV.com |date=July 14, 2010 |url= http://www.mtv.com/news/articles/1643645/20100714/story.jhtml|access-date=July 22, 2010|archive-date=July 20, 2010|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100720012011/http://www.mtv.com/news/articles/1643645/20100714/story.jhtml|url-status=dead}}</ref> This sequence was filmed on and off for months, with the van being shot out of a cannon, according to actor Dileep Rao. Capturing the actors suspended within the van in slow motion took a whole day to film.

Once the van landed in the water, the challenge for the actors was to avoid panic. "And when they ask you to act, it's a bit of an ask," explained [[Cillian Murphy]].<ref name="Ditzian" /> The actors had to be underwater for four to five minutes while drawing air from [[Diving cylinder|scuba tanks]]; underwater [[buddy breathing]] is shown in this sequence.<ref name="Ditzian" />

The final phase of principal photography took place in [[Alberta]] in late November 2009. The location manager discovered a temporarily closed ski resort, [[Fortress Mountain Resort|Fortress Mountain]].<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|22}} An elaborate set was assembled near the top station of the Canadian [[chairlift]], taking three months to build.<ref name= Jolin />{{rp|93}} The production had to wait for a huge snowstorm, which eventually arrived.<ref name="Hiscock" /> The ski-chase sequence was inspired by Nolan's favorite [[James Bond]] film, ''[[On Her Majesty's Secret Service (film)|On Her Majesty's Secret Service]]'' (1969): "What I liked about it that we've tried to emulate in this film is there's a tremendous balance in that movie of action and scale and romanticism and tragedy and emotion."<ref name= Jolin />{{rp|91}}

=== Cinematography ===
The film was shot primarily in the [[anamorphic format]] on [[35 mm movie film|35 mm film]], with key sequences filmed on [[65 mm]], and aerial sequences in [[VistaVision]]. Nolan did not shoot any footage with [[IMAX]] cameras as he had with ''[[The Dark Knight]]''. "We didn't feel that we were going to be able to shoot in IMAX because of the size of the cameras because this film, given that it deals with a potentially surreal area, the nature of dreams and so forth, I wanted it to be as realistic as possible. Not be bound by the scale of those IMAX cameras, even though I love the format dearly".<ref name="Weintraub" /> In addition Nolan and Pfister tested using [[Showscan]] and [[List of motion picture film formats|Super Dimension 70]] as potential large-format, [[high frame rate|high-frame-rate]] camera systems to use for the film, but ultimately decided against either format.<ref name= Heuring />{{rp|29}}

Sequences in slow motion were filmed on a Photo-Sonics 35&nbsp;mm camera at speeds of up to 1,000 frames per second. Wally Pfister tested shooting some of these sequences using a high speed [[Digital cinematography|digital camera]], but found the format to be too unreliable due to technical glitches. "Out of six times that we shot on the digital format, we only had one usable piece and it didn't end up in the film. Out of the six times we shot with the Photo-Sonics camera and 35 mm running through it, every single shot was in the movie."<ref name="Kodak">{{Cite news|title=From The Dark Knight to Inception, Wally Pfister, ASC refuses to compromise| publisher= Kodak |url= http://motion.kodak.com/motion/Products/Customer_Testimonials/Wally_Pfister/index.htm#ixzz2Ti47T2NZ|access-date=May 19, 2013|archive-date=May 23, 2013 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130523095937/http://motion.kodak.com/motion/Products/Customer_Testimonials/Wally_Pfister/index.htm#ixzz2Ti47T2NZ|url-status=live}}</ref>

Nolan also chose not to shoot any of the film in [[3D film|3D]] as he prefers shooting on film<ref name="Weintraub" /> using [[prime lens]]es, which is not possible with 3D cameras.<ref name="Playlist">{{Cite news|title=Christopher Nolan Tested 3D Conversion For 'Inception,' Might Use Process For 'Batman 3'|work=The Playlist|date=June 14, 2010|url=https://theplaylist.blogspot.com/2010/06/christopher-nolan-tested-3d-conversion.html|access-date=January 22, 2011|archive-date=May 10, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110510064735/http://theplaylist.blogspot.com/2010/06/christopher-nolan-tested-3d-conversion.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Nolan has also criticized the dim image that 3D projection produces, and disputes that traditional film does not allow realistic [[depth perception]], saying "I think it's a misnomer to call it 3D versus 2D. The whole point of cinematic imagery is it's three dimensional... You know 95% of our [[depth perception|depth cues]] come from [[Ambient occlusion|occlusion]], resolution, color and so forth, so the idea of calling a 2D movie a '2D movie' is a little misleading."<ref name="latimes-hcff">{{cite news|url=http://herocomplex.latimes.com/2010/06/13/christopher-nolan-inception-3d-dark-knight-hollywood/|title=Christopher Nolan's dim view of a Hollywood craze: 'I'm not a huge fan of 3-D'|date=June 13, 2010|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|access-date=January 22, 2011|archive-date=February 1, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110201044444/http://herocomplex.latimes.com/2010/06/13/christopher-nolan-inception-3d-dark-knight-hollywood/|url-status=live}}</ref> Nolan did test [[2D to 3D conversion|converting]] ''Inception'' into 3D in post-production but decided that, while it was possible, he lacked the time to complete the conversion to a standard he was happy with.<ref name="Hiscock" /><ref name="latimes-hcff" /> In February 2011 [[Jonathan Liebesman]] suggested that Warner Bros. were attempting a 3D conversion for [[Blu-ray]] release.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.movieweb.com/news/inception-being-converted-to-3d-blu-ray|title=''Inception'' being converted to 3D Blu-ray?|first= Brian |last= Gallagher |date=February 24, 2011 |access-date=February 27, 2011 |website=[[MovieWeb]] |archive-date=February 26, 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110226041904/http://www.movieweb.com/news/inception-being-converted-to-3d-blu-ray|url-status=live}}</ref>

Wally Pfister gave each location and dream level a distinctive look to aid the audience's recognition of the narrative's location during the heavily crosscut portion of the film: the mountain fortress appears sterile and cool, the hotel hallways have warm hues, and the scenes in the van are more neutral.<ref name= Heuring />{{rp|35–36}}

Nolan has said that the film "deals with levels of reality, and perceptions of reality which is something I'm very interested in. It's an action film set in a contemporary world, but with a slight science-fiction bent to it", while also describing it as "very much an ensemble film structured somewhat as a heist movie. It's an action adventure that spans the globe".<ref>{{Cite news|title=''Inception''|work=[[Empire (magazine)|Empire]]|date=April 2010}}</ref>

=== Visual effects ===
For dream sequences in ''Inception'', Nolan used little [[computer-generated imagery|CGI]], preferring [[practical effect]]s whenever possible. Nolan said, "It's always very important to me to do as much as possible in-camera, and then, if necessary, computer graphics are very useful to build on or enhance what you have achieved physically."<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|12}} To this end, visual effects supervisor [[Paul Franklin (visual effects supervisor)|Paul Franklin]] built [[Miniature effect|miniatures]] of the mountain fortress set and then blew it up for the film. For the fight scene that takes place in zero gravity, he used CGI-based effects to "subtly bend elements like physics, space and time."<ref name="trussell">{{Cite news|last=Russell|first=Terrence|title=How ''Inception''{{'}}s Astonishing Visuals Came to Life|magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]|date=July 20, 2010|url=https://www.wired.com/underwire/2010/07/inception-visual-effects|access-date=July 21, 2010|archive-date=September 13, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120913044009/http://www.wired.com/underwire/2010/07/inception-visual-effects|url-status=live}}</ref>

The most challenging effect was the "Limbo" city level at the end of the film, because it continually developed during production. Franklin had artists build concepts while Nolan expressed his ideal vision: "Something glacial, with clear modernist architecture, but with chunks of it breaking off into the sea like icebergs".<ref name="trussell" /> Franklin and his team ended up with "something that looked like an iceberg version of [[Gotham City]] with water running through it."<ref name="trussell" /> They created a basic model of a glacier and then designers created a program that added elements like roads, intersections and ravines until they had a complex, yet organic-looking, cityscape. For the Paris-folding sequence, Franklin had artists producing concept sketches and then they created rough computer animations to give them an idea of what the sequence looked like while in motion. Later during principal photography, Nolan was able to direct DiCaprio and Page based on this rough computer animation that Franklin had created. ''Inception'' had nearly 500 visual effects shots (in comparison, ''Batman Begins'' had approximately 620), which is relatively few in comparison to contemporary effects-heavy films, which can have as many as 2,000 visual effects shots.<ref name="trussell" />

== Music ==
{{Main|Inception: Music from the Motion Picture}}

The score for ''Inception'' was composed and arranged by [[Hans Zimmer]],<ref name="CinemaRewind" /> who described his work as "a very electronic,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://screenrant.com/inception-score-hans-zimmers-mikee-65200 |title=Hans Zimmer's 'Inception' Score Will Release On July 13th | website= ScreenRant.com |access-date=July 1, 2010 |date=June 18, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100625130549/http://screenrant.com/inception-score-hans-zimmers-mikee-65200/ |archive-date=June 25, 2010}}</ref> dense score",<ref name="Cassidy" /> filled with "nostalgia and sadness" to match Cobb's feelings throughout the film.<ref name="Martens" /> The music was written simultaneously to filming,<ref name="Cassidy">{{cite news |last=Cassidy |first=Kevin |title=Q&A: Composer Hans Zimmer |work=[[The Hollywood Reporter]] |date=July 13, 2010 |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/qampa-composer-hans-zimmer-25455 |access-date=July 14, 2010 |archive-date=November 2, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121102202043/http://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/qampa-composer-hans-zimmer-25455 |url-status=live }}</ref> and features a guitar sound reminiscent of [[Ennio Morricone]], played by [[Johnny Marr]], former guitarist of [[the Smiths]].
[[Édith Piaf]]'s "[[Non, je ne regrette rien]]" ("No, I Regret Nothing") appears throughout the film, used to accurately time the dreams, and Zimmer reworked pieces of the song into cues of the score.<ref name="Martens">{{cite news |last=Martens |first=Todd |title=Hans Zimmer and Johnny Marr talk about the sad romance of 'Inception' |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=July 20, 2010 |url=http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/herocomplex/2010/07/inception-christopher-nolan-the-smiths-johnny-marr-hans-zimmer-and-johnny-marr-on-the-sound-of-inception-its-about-sadness.html |access-date=July 20, 2010 |archive-date=July 21, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100721234310/http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/herocomplex/2010/07/inception-christopher-nolan-the-smiths-johnny-marr-hans-zimmer-and-johnny-marr-on-the-sound-of-inception-its-about-sadness.html |url-status=live }}</ref>
A [[Inception: Music from the Motion Picture|soundtrack album]] was released on July 11, 2010, by [[Reprise Records]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.inceptionscore.com/|title=Inception: Music from the Motion Picture official website|publisher=Warner Bros.| website= insceptionscore.com| access-date=July 3, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120616131408/http://www.inceptionscore.com/|archive-date=June 16, 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref> The majority of the score was also included in high resolution [[5.1 surround sound]] on the second disc of the two-disc Blu-ray release.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.blu-ray.com/movies/Inception-Blu-ray/14492/#Review|title=Inception Blu-ray review from Blu-ray.com|access-date=August 8, 2012|archive-date=August 15, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120815212509/http://www.blu-ray.com/movies/Inception-Blu-ray/14492/#Review|url-status=live}}</ref> Hans Zimmer's music was nominated for an Academy Award in the [[Academy Award for Best Original Score|Best Original Score]] category in 2011, losing to [[Trent Reznor]] and [[Atticus Ross]] of ''[[The Social Network]]''.<ref name=oscars />

== Themes ==

=== Reality and dreams ===
[[File: Impossible staircase.svg|right|thumb|[[Penrose stairs]] are incorporated into the film as an example of the [[impossible object]]s that can be created in [[lucid dream]] worlds.|alt=A staircase in a square format. The stairs make four 90-degree turns in each corner, so they are in the format of a continuous loop.]]
In ''Inception'', Nolan wanted to explore "the idea of people sharing a dream space... That gives you the ability to access somebody's [[unconscious mind]]. What would that be used and abused for?"<ref name="Weintraub">{{Cite news|last=Weintraub |first=Steve |title=Christopher Nolan and Emma Thomas Interview | website= Collider.com |date=March 25, 2010 |url=https://collider.com/director-christopher-nolan-and-producer-emma-thomas-interview-inception-they-talk-3d-what-kind-of-cameras-they-used-pre-viz-wb-and-a-lot-more/ |access-date=April 6, 2010 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100327204348/http://www.collider.com/2010/03/25/director-christopher-nolan-and-producer-emma-thomas-interview-inception-they-talk-3d-what-kind-of-cameras-they-used-pre-viz-wb-and-a-lot-more/ |archive-date=March 27, 2010 }}</ref> The majority of the film's plot takes place in these interconnected dream worlds. This structure creates a framework where actions in the real or dream worlds ripple across others. The dream is always in a state of production, and shifts across the levels as the characters navigate it.<ref name='Paul'>Paul, I. A. [http://sensesofcinema.com/2010/feature-articles/desiring-machines-in-american-cinema-what-inception-tells-us-about-our-experience-of-reality-and-film/ Desiring-Machines in American Cinema: What Inception tells us about our experience of reality and film] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110824032553/http://www.sensesofcinema.com/2010/feature-articles/desiring-machines-in-american-cinema-what-inception-tells-us-about-our-experience-of-reality-and-film/ |date=August 24, 2011 }} ''Senses of Cinema'', Issue 56. Retrieved October 4, 2011</ref> By contrast, the world of ''[[The Matrix]]'' (1999) is an authoritarian, computer-controlled one, alluding to theories of social control developed by thinkers [[Michel Foucault]] and [[Jean Baudrillard]]. However, according to one interpretation Nolan's world has more in common with the works of [[Gilles Deleuze]] and [[Félix Guattari]].<ref name='Paul' />

[[David Denby]] in ''[[The New Yorker]]'' compared Nolan's cinematic treatment of dreams to [[Luis Buñuel]]'s in ''[[Belle de Jour (film)|Belle de Jour]]'' (1967) and ''[[The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie]]'' (1972).<ref name="Denby" /> He criticized Nolan's "literal-minded" action level sequencing compared to Buñuel, who "silently pushed us into reveries and left us alone to enjoy our wonderment, but Nolan is working on so many levels of representation at once that he has to lay in pages of dialogue just to explain what's going on." The latter captures "the peculiar malign intensity of actual dreams."<ref name="Denby" />

[[Deirdre Barrett]], a dream researcher at [[Harvard University]], said that Nolan did not get every detail accurate regarding dreams, but their illogical, rambling, disjointed plots would not make for a great thriller anyway. However, "he did get many aspects right," she said, citing the scene in which a sleeping Cobb is shoved into a full bath, and in the dream world water gushes into the windows of the building, waking him up. "That's very much how real stimuli get incorporated, and you very often wake up right after that intrusion."<ref name="Breznican">{{Cite news|last=Breznican|first=Anthony|title=With ''Inception'', Chris Nolan's head games continue|work=[[USA Today]]|date=July 15, 2010|url=https://www.usatoday.com/life/movies/news/2010-07-15-inception15_CV_N.htm|access-date=July 15, 2010|archive-date=June 29, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120629093837/http://www.usatoday.com/life/movies/news/2010-07-15-inception15_CV_N.htm|url-status=live}}</ref>

Nolan himself said, "I tried to work that idea of manipulation and management of a [[Lucid dream|conscious dream]] being a skill that these people have. Really the script is based on those common, very basic experiences and concepts, and where can those take you? And the only outlandish idea that the film presents, really, is the existence of a technology that allows you to enter and share the same dream as someone else."<ref name="Boucher" />

=== Dreams and cinema ===
Others have argued that the film is itself a [[oneiric (film theory)|metaphor for filmmaking]], and that the filmgoing experience itself, images flashing before one's eyes in a darkened room, is akin to a dream. Writing in ''Wired'', Jonah Lehrer supported this interpretation and presented neurological evidence that brain activity is strikingly similar during film-watching and sleeping. In both, the [[visual cortex]] is highly active and the [[prefrontal cortex]], which deals with logic, deliberate analysis, and self-awareness, is quiet.<ref name='Lehrer'>[[Jonah Lehrer|Lehrer, J.]] [https://www.wired.com/wiredscience/2010/07/the-neuroscience-of-inception/ The Neuroscience of Inception] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140316015717/http://www.wired.com/wiredscience/2010/07/the-neuroscience-of-inception |date=March 16, 2014 }}, ''Wired'', July 26, 2010. Retrieved October 8, 2011.</ref>

Paul argued that the experience of going to a picturehouse is itself an exercise in shared dreaming, particularly when viewing ''Inception'': the film's sharp cutting between scenes forces the viewer to create larger narrative arcs to stitch the pieces together. This demand of production parallel to consumption of the images, on the part of the audience is analogous to dreaming itself. As in the film's story, in a cinema one enters into the space of another's dream, in this case Nolan's, as with any work of art, one's reading of it is ultimately influenced by one's own subjective desires and subconscious.<ref name="Paul" /> At Bir-Hakeim bridge in Paris, Ariadne creates an illusion of infinity by adding [[Infinity mirror|facing mirrors]] underneath its struts, Stephanie Dreyfus in ''la Croix'' asked "Is this not a strong, beautiful metaphor for the cinema and its power of illusion?"<ref>Dreyfus, Stéphanie [http://www.la-croix.com/Culture-Loisirs/Culture/Actualite/Inception-allegorie-onirique-sur-l-illusion-cinematographique-_NG_-2010-07-20-554535 "Inception", allégorie onirique sur l'illusion cinématographique] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170225212142/http://www.la-croix.com/Culture-Loisirs/Culture/Actualite/Inception-allegorie-onirique-sur-l-illusion-cinematographique-_NG_-2010-07-20-554535 |date=February 25, 2017 }} ''[[La Croix (newspaper)|La Croix]]'', July 20, 2010. Retrieved January 3, 2012</ref>

== Cinematic technique ==
{{See also|Cinematic style of Christopher Nolan}}

=== Genre ===
Nolan combined elements from several different film genres into the film, notably science fiction, [[heist film]], and [[film noir]].
[[Marion Cotillard]] plays "Mal" Cobb, Dom Cobb's projection of his guilt over his deceased wife's suicide. As the film's main antagonist, she is a frequent, malevolent presence in his dreams. Dom is unable to control these projections of her, challenging his abilities as an extractor.<ref name="threecircle" /> Nolan described Mal as "the essence of the femme fatale",<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|9}} the key ''noir'' reference in the film. As a "classic femme fatale" her relationship with Cobb is in his mind, a manifestation of Cobb's own neurosis and fear of how little he knows about the woman he loves.<ref name="wired-jan11" /> DiCaprio praised Cotillard's performance saying that "she can be strong and vulnerable and hopeful and heartbreaking all in the same moment, which was perfect for all the contradictions of her character".<ref name= ProdNotes6-18 />{{rp|10}}

Nolan began with the structure of a heist movie, since [[Exposition (literary technique)|exposition]] is an essential element of that genre, though adapted it to have a greater emotional narrative suited to the world of dreams and subconscious.<ref name="wired-jan11" /> As Denby described this device: "the outer shell of the story is an elaborate caper".<ref name="Denby" /> [[Kristin Thompson]] argued that exposition was a major formal device in the film. While a traditional heist movie has a heavy dose of exposition at the beginning as the team assembles and the leader explains the plan, in ''Inception'' this becomes nearly continuous as the group progresses through the various levels of dreaming.<ref name= Bordwell2>{{cite web| url= http://www.davidbordwell.net/blog/2010/08/12/revisiting-inception/ |title= Revisiting Inception| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180929084828/http://www.davidbordwell.net/blog/2010/08/12/revisiting-inception/ |archive-date=September 29, 2018 |work= Observations on Film Art |format= blog |first2= David| last2= Bordwell| first1= Kristin |last1= Thompson| publisher= David Bordwell |date= August 12, 2010| access-date= October 6, 2011}}</ref> Three quarters of the film, until the van begins to fall from the bridge, are devoted to explaining its plot. In this way, exposition takes precedence over characterization. The characters' relationships are created by their respective skills and roles. Ariadne, like [[Ariadne|her ancient namesake]], creates the maze and guides the others through it, but also helps Cobb navigate his own subconscious, and as the sole student of dream sharing, helps the audience understand the concept of the plot.<ref name='Bordwell1'>{{cite web| url= http://www.davidbordwell.net/blog/2010/08/06/inception-or-dream-a-little-dream-within-a-dream-with-me/ |title= Inception; or, Dream a Little Dream within a Dream with Me| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20111007035606/http://www.davidbordwell.net/blog/2010/08/06/inception-or-dream-a-little-dream-within-a-dream-with-me/ |archive-date=October 7, 2011 |work= Observations on Film Art |format= blog |first2= David| last2= Bordwell| first1= Kristin |last1= Thompson| publisher= David Bordwell |date= August 6, 2010| access-date= October 6, 2011}}</ref>

Nolan drew inspiration from the works of [[Jorge Luis Borges]],<ref name="Hiscock" /><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thestar.com/article/836236--howell-relax-and-enjoy-the-ride-inception-director-says|title=Howell: Relax and enjoy the ride, Inception director says| first= Peter| last= Howell |date=July 15, 2010|work=Toronto Star|access-date=September 4, 2010|archive-date=July 16, 2010|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100716232640/http://www.thestar.com/article/836236--howell-relax-and-enjoy-the-ride-inception-director-says| url-status=live}}</ref> including "[[The Secret Miracle]]" and "[[The Circular Ruins]]",<ref name="Revisit Inception">{{Cite news| last= Ouellette| first= Jennifer|date=2020-09-07|title=Can't watch Tenet? Now is the perfect time to revisit Inception |url= https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2020/09/cant-watch-tenet-now-is-the-perfect-time-to-revisit-inception/|access-date=2020-09-07| website= Ars Technica| language=en-us|archive-date=September 7, 2020|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200907155246/https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2020/09/cant-watch-tenet-now-is-the-perfect-time-to-revisit-inception/ |url-status= live}}</ref> and from the films ''[[Blade Runner]]'' (1982) and ''[[The Matrix]]'' (1999).<ref name="Revisit Inception" /><ref>{{cite web|title=Inception par Christopher Nolan: Interview, références, indices..| website= Excessif.com |url= http://www.excessif.com/cinema/actu-cinema/dossiers/inception-par-christopher-nolan-interview-references-indices-5926972-760.html|access-date= January 4, 2010| url-status= dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100717005841/http://www.excessif.com/cinema/actu-cinema/dossiers/inception-par-christopher-nolan-interview-references-indices-5926972-760.html|archive-date=July 17, 2010| language=fr}}</ref> While Nolan has not confirmed this, it has also been suggested by many observers that the movie draws heavy inspiration from the 2006 animated film ''[[Paprika (2006 film)|Paprika]]''.<ref name="Drazen">{{cite book |last=Drazen |first=Patrick |title=Anime Explosion!: The What? Why? and Wow! of Japanese Animation, Revised and Updated Edition |date=2014 |publisher=[[Stone Bridge Press]] |isbn=978-1-61172-550-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-s30AgAAQBAJ&pg=PA339}}</ref><ref name="Wardlow" /><ref name="IGN" />

=== Ending ===
The film cuts to the [[closing credits]] from a shot of the top apparently starting to show an ever so faint wobble, inviting speculation about whether the final sequence was reality or another dream. Nolan confirmed that the ambiguity was deliberate,<ref name="wired-jan11">{{cite magazine| url= https://www.wired.com/2010/11/pl_inception_nolan/all/|title=Inception's director discusses the film's ending and creation |last= Capps |first= Robert |date=December 8, 2010|magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]|access-date=January 24, 2011|archive-date=September 27, 2017|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170927041150/https://www.wired.com/2010/11/pl_inception_nolan/all/|url-status=live}}</ref> saying, "I've been asked the question more times than I've ever been asked any other question about any other film I've made... What's funny to me is that people really do expect me to answer it."<ref name="insidemovies">{{cite magazine|url=http://insidemovies.ew.com/2010/11/30/christopher-nolan-batman-inception/|title=Christopher Nolan on his 'last' Batman movie, an 'Inception' videogame, and that spinning top|last=Jensen|first=Jeff|date=November 30, 2010|magazine=Entertainment Weekly|access-date=January 6, 2011|archive-date=December 2, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101202065701/http://insidemovies.ew.com/2010/11/30/christopher-nolan-batman-inception/|url-status=live}}</ref> The film's script concludes with "Behind him, on the table, the spinning top is STILL SPINNING. And we—FADE OUT".<ref>{{Cite book|title=Inception – The Shooting Script| first= Christopher |last= Nolan|date=August 17, 2010|page=218|isbn=978-1-60887-015-8|publisher=Insight Editions}}</ref> Nolan said, "I put that cut there at the end, imposing an ambiguity from outside the film. That always felt the right ending to me—it always felt like the appropriate 'kick' to me... The real point of the scene—and this is what I tell people—is that Cobb isn't looking at the top. He's looking at his kids. He's left it behind. That's the emotional significance of the thing."<ref name="insidemovies" />

Caine interpreted the ending as meaning that Cobb is in the real world, quoting Nolan as telling him "'Well, when you're in the scene, it's reality.' So get that — if I'm in it, it's reality. If I'm not in it, it's a dream". While reiterating that he was uncomfortable with definitively explaining the scene, Nolan in 2023 credited [[Emma Thomas]] as providing "the correct answer, which is Leo's character ... doesn't care at that point".<ref name="sharf20230721">{{Cite magazine |last=Sharf |first=Zack |date=2023-07-21 |title=Christopher Nolan Tells the 'Correct Answer' to 'Inception' Ending, Recalls Sneaking Into Theaters and Hearing 'Gasps, Groans, Frustrations' |url=https://variety.com/2023/film/news/christopher-nolan-inception-ending-correct-answer-1235676875/ |magazine=Variety |language=en-US |access-date=2023-07-22 |archive-date=July 22, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230722100930/https://variety.com/2023/film/news/christopher-nolan-inception-ending-correct-answer-1235676875/ |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Mark Fisher]] argued that "a century of cultural theory" cautions against accepting the [[authorial intent|author's interpretation]] as anything more than a supplementary text, and this all the more so given the theme of the instability of any one master position in Nolan's films. Therein the manipulator is often the one who ends up manipulated, and Cobb's "not caring" about whether or not his world is real may be the price of his happiness and release.<ref>Fisher, Mark "[https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.1525/fq.2011.64.3.37 The Lost Unconscious: Delusions and Dreams in ''Inception''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190101100606/https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.1525/fq.2011.64.3.37 |date=January 1, 2019 }}", ''[[Film Quarterly]]'', Vol. 64, No. 3 (Spring 2011), pp. 37–45 University of California Press.</ref>

== Release ==

=== Marketing ===
Warner Bros. spent US$100&nbsp;million marketing the film. Although ''Inception'' was not part of an existing franchise, Sue Kroll, president of Warner's worldwide marketing, said the company believed it could gain awareness due to the strength of "Christopher Nolan as a brand". Kroll declared that "We don't have the brand equity that usually drives a big summer opening, but we have a great cast and a fresh idea from a filmmaker with a track record of making incredible movies. If you can't make those elements work, it's a sad day."<ref name="Fritz2">{{Cite news|last=Fritz|first=Ben|title=Warner gambles on an unproven commodity|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=July 7, 2010|url=https://www.latimes.com/business/la-fi-ct-inception-20100713, 0,3119222.story|access-date=July 13, 2010|archive-date=July 28, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100728142042/http://www.latimes.com/business/la-fi-ct-inception-20100713, 0,3119222.story|url-status=live}}</ref> The studio also tried to maintain a campaign of secrecy—as reported by the Senior VP of Interactive Marketing, Michael Tritter, "You have this movie which is going to have a pretty big built in fanbase... but you also have a movie that you are trying to keep very secret. Chris [Nolan] really likes people to see his movies in a theater and not see it all beforehand so everything that you do to market that—at least early on—is with an eye to feeding the interest to fans."<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.kcrw.com/etc/programs/tb/tb100816finding_salt_marketi|title=Finding 'Salt;' Marketing 'Inception'| website= [[KCRW]].com |date=June 18, 2010|access-date=July 4, 2011|archive-date=September 23, 2010|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100923172158/http://www.kcrw.com/etc/programs/tb/tb100816finding_salt_marketi| url-status= live}}</ref>

A [[viral marketing]] campaign was employed for the film. After the revelation of the first teaser trailer, in August 2009, the film's official website featured only an animation of Cobb's spinning top. In December, the top toppled over and the website opened the online game ''Mind Crime'', which upon completion revealed ''Inception''{{'}}s poster.<ref>{{cite ''Inception'' and its film trailers are widely credited for launching the trend throughout the 2010s in which blockbuster movie trailers repeatedly hit audiences with so-called "[[BRAAAM|braam]]" sounds: "bassy, brassy, thunderous notes—like a foghorn on steroids—meant to impart a sense of apocalyptic momentousness".<ref name="Abramovitch">{{cite news |last1= Abramovitch |first1= Seth |title='Braaams' for Beginners: How a Horn Sound Ate Hollywood |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/braaams-beginners-how-a-horn-793220 |work= The Hollywood Reporter |publisher=Prometheus Global Media |date=5 May 2015 |access-date=May 26, 2020 |archive-date=June 5, 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200605141721/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/braaams-beginners-how-a-horn-793220 |url-status=live }}</ref> However, different composers worked on the teaser trailer, first trailer, second trailer, and film score, meaning that identifying the composer(s) responsible for that trend is a complicated task.<ref name="Abramovitch" />

=== Putative video game{{anchor|Proposed video game}} ===
In a November 2010 interview, Nolan expressed his intention to develop a video game set in the ''Inception'' world, working with a team of collaborators. He described it as "a longer-term proposition", referring to the medium of video games as "something I've wanted to explore".<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Jensen|first=Jeff|title=Christopher Nolan on his 'last' Batman movie, an 'Inception' videogame, and that spinning top|url=http://insidemovies.ew.com/2010/11/30/christopher-nolan-batman-inception/|magazine=Entertainment Weekly|access-date=December 3, 2010|date=November 30, 2010|archive-date=December 2, 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101202065701/http://insidemovies.ew.com/2010/11/30/christopher-nolan-batman-inception/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== 10th anniversary re-release ===
''Inception'' was re-released in theaters for its tenth anniversary, starting on August 12, 2020, in international markets and on August 21 in the U.S.<ref name="TenetDelaySep3">{{Cite web |url=https://deadline.com/2020/07/tenet-sets-worldwide-release-dates-u-s-labor-day-weekend-1202995899/ |title='Tenet' Rollout Set: 70 Countries To Begin Opening By End Of August, Followed By U.S. Over Labor Day Weekend |last=D'Alessandro |first=Anthony |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]] |date=July 27, 2020 |access-date=July 29, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200729175953/https://deadline.com/2020/07/tenet-sets-worldwide-release-dates-u-s-labor-day-weekend-1202995899/ |archive-date=July 29, 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref> The re-release was originally announced by Warner Bros. in June 2020 and scheduled for July 17, 2020, taking the original release date for Nolan's upcoming film ''[[Tenet]]'' after its delay to July 31 due to the impact of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] on movie theaters.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://deadline.com/2020/06/tenet-release-date-change-to-july-31-1202938871/ |title='Tenet' Moves To July 31; 10th Anniversary Reissue Of Christopher Nolan's 'Inception' To Go On July 17 |last=D'Alessandro |first=Anthony |website=[[Deadline Hollywood]] |date=June 12, 2020 |access-date=14 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200613131535/https://deadline.com/2020/06/tenet-release-date-change-to-july-31-1202938871/ |archive-date=13 June 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref> After ''Tenet'' was delayed again to August 12, the re-release was shifted to July 31,<ref name="Rubin-Jun2020">{{cite web|last=Rubin|first=Rebecca|date=June 25, 2020|url=https://variety.com/2020/film/box-office/tenet-release-date-delayed-again-christopher-nolan-1234690272/|title=Christopher Nolan's 'Tenet' Delays Release Date Again|website=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200626161602/https://variety.com/2020/film/box-office/tenet-release-date-delayed-again-christopher-nolan-1234690272/|archive-date=June 26, 2020|url-status=live|access-date=June 27, 2020 }}</ref> before setting on the August release date following a third delay.<ref name="TenetDelaySep3" />
